Do not confuse receiving BPDUs on a blocked port with forwarding ordinary data: blocked ports still need to hear control information.

sections.title: The three elections and a cost worked example
sections.html:
1. Root bridge: the lowest Bridge ID wins. The simplified ID comprises priority then MAC address; default configurable priority is 32768 in steps of 4096. Priority is compared before MAC. In Cisco per-VLAN output, the system-ID extension includes the VLAN ID, so VLAN 1 can display 32769 or 4097 for a configured base priority 32768 or 4096.

2. Root port: each non-root switch selects the port giving lowest total path cost to the root. 3. Designated port: each segment selects the port advertising the best path/root information; other redundant ports block/discard. The lecture emphasizes cost; equal-cost decisions then compare bridge/port identifiers rather than choosing arbitrarily. The root has designated ports and no root port.

Link speedShort path cost used by the lecture

Lecture example: A’s direct 100 Mbps path costs 19; through B it costs 19+4=23, so A selects direct. B’s direct gigabit path costs 4; through A costs 19+19=38, so B also selects direct. On the A–B segment, B advertises root cost 4 and A advertises 19, so B is designated and A’s port on that segment blocks. Root-port selection and designated-port selection answer different questions.

Disabled/down is another operational state, although the tutorial asks for these four progressive states. Classic 802.1D uses timers and can take roughly 30–50 seconds to recover in the lab’s failure conditions. RSTP’s discarding state combines non-forwarding behavior; rapid convergence uses defined roles and proposal/agreement on suitable links, not simply a universal removal of all timing checks.

An alternate port is a standby route toward the root via another bridge; a backup port is redundancy for a designated port on the same shared segment. These are not identical. The supplied Packet Tracer lab supports pvst and rapid-pvst; it explicitly says standalone IEEE RSTP mode/MSTP configuration is unavailable in its environment. Actual command support can depend on the chosen simulator/device version.

sections.title: Three attack mechanisms and their distinct impacts
sections.html:
AttackMechanismImpact
Root bridge manipulationAdvertise a superior Bridge ID/low priority through unauthenticated BPDUs; force the network to build around an unauthorized root.Path manipulation, instability and potentially interception or DoS.
Topology Change flooding/spoofingRepeated false topology-change messages or link transitions keep forwarding information aging/flushing excessively.Unknown-unicast flooding, degraded performance and possible traffic exposure without becoming root.
STP DoSHigh BPDU load and/or changing claims consume control-plane work and repeatedly trigger reconvergence.Resource exhaustion and network availability loss.

Root election alone does not guarantee every frame flows through the rogue device: actual interception needs an appropriate transit position/links and depends on resulting port roles. The lecture’s “traffic through attacker” is a risk scenario, not a universal consequence of winning with a single edge connection. Classical TC handling commonly shortens MAC aging, while rapid variants handle changes differently; the shared result is frequent relearning/flooding. This resembles CAM flooding’s symptom but uses repeated invalidation rather than filling memory with invented addresses.

sections.title: Six features: match placement and purpose
sections.html:
FeaturePlacementTrigger/actionLimits
Root GuardDesignated ports toward downstream devices that must not become root.A superior BPDU puts the port into root-inconsistent non-forwarding condition.Blocks superior root claims; does not reject every BPDU/TC message.
BPDU GuardEnd-host access ports, usually with PortFast.Any received BPDU causes err-disable.Do not apply indiscriminately to legitimate inter-switch links.
BPDU FilterCarefully chosen ports excluded from BPDU participation; lab compares one PC-facing port.Interface-level form neither sends nor accepts BPDUs and leaves data forwarding up.Hides the signal and can permit loops; not equivalent protection to Guard.
Loop GuardRoot/alternate/non-designated ports on suitable inter-switch links.Unexpected BPDU loss holds a port loop-inconsistent rather than letting it forward.Protects BPDU-loss/unidirectional-failure cases, not general malicious BPDU floods.
BackboneFastSwitch-wide classic-STP feature; lab configures distribution switches.Accelerates recovery from indirect failures instead of waiting the full Max Age delay.Convergence optimization; not BPDU authentication.
UplinkFastSwitch-wide on suitable access switches with redundant uplinks.Direct root-uplink failure rapidly promotes an alternate uplink.Classic-STP optimization; rapid protocols already incorporate fast recovery.

PortFast expedites a known edge port’s transition; it is not itself a rogue-switch rejection policy. Root Guard and Loop Guard protect different assumptions and should not be placed on the same port as interchangeable options.

sections.title: BPDU Guard versus Filter: a necessary qualification
sections.html:
The supplied lecture contrasts visible shutdown/err-disable by Guard with silent ignore by Filter. That is a useful observation in its single-rogue-switch lab. However, interface-level spanning-tree bpdufilter enable effectively removes STP protection on that interface; it can enable a bridging loop if an extra path appears. Global PortFast-default filtering has different fallback behavior when a BPDU arrives. For ordinary corporate host ports, Guard is generally the stronger choice because unexpected BPDUs trigger containment and investigation. See Cisco’s BPDU Filter command guidance.

Use the Filter exercise only in the course’s isolated comparison topology and remove the temporary rogue switch when finished. The experiment shows two different BPDU responses; it does not establish that ignoring all BPDUs is universally safe. Loop Guard protects missing expected BPDUs on infrastructure links, so it cannot substitute for edge BPDU Guard against the three fabricated-message attacks.

sections.title: Lab Part 1: observe root/blocked ports and measure recovery
sections.html:
Run show spanning-tree vlan 1 on all five switches before choosing a root. Record the actual Root ID and local Bridge ID. Equal default priorities mean the lowest MAC breaks the initial election tie, so the root cannot be inferred from names such as C1. Record actual root ports, designated ports and blocking/discarding ports. Screenshot at least two outputs showing the root and a blocked port.

On D1/D2’s Gi0/2 backbone, compare their advertised root path cost; lower cost wins designated. If costs tie, compare Bridge IDs. Conditional example: after C1 is deliberately root and gigabit core links cost 4, both distribution switches advertise cost 4. The lower-ID D1/D2 wins designated on their shared backbone, with the other port alternate/blocking. Access-to-distribution links involving Fa ports negotiate 100 Mbps in the illustrated design: cost 19 plus distribution root cost 4 gives access path cost 23. Verify actual negotiated speeds/costs rather than assuming a port name determines the whole link.

Begin repeated pings PC1 → 192.168.1.20. Disconnect the same chosen A1 uplink, count losses/elapsed time until recovery, reconnect and allow stabilization. Classic PVST+ often loses roughly 30–50 seconds, but record your measured value. Failed-ping count approximates seconds only if interval/timing is about one second. If -t is unavailable in the Packet Tracer PC, repeat pings or use simulation/time observations. Then configure every switch with spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst, repeat the identical failure test, and record actual rapid recovery. Do not invent results or screenshots.

sections.html:
Keep Rapid PVST+ enabled. Set C1 base priority to 4096; this selects it over the other default-priority devices, not over every conceivable lower-priority rogue. Root Guard is the layer that rejects superior downstream claims. Configure Root Guard on D1/D2 Fa0/1–2 toward access; Guard plus PortFast on A1’s PC port; Filter plus PortFast on A2’s comparison port; Loop Guard on both access uplinks; UplinkFast on both access switches; BackboneFast on both distribution switches.

Every switch:

end

The supplied lab includes UplinkFast/BackboneFast for familiarity and status verification. They were designed for classic STP, and Rapid PVST+ already provides rapid recovery. Command acceptance/status varies by simulated device/software; do not claim a measured improvement from those features without evidence. The file provides no MSTP command sequence to execute in this Packet Tracer environment.

sections.title: Lab verification, connectivity and rogue-switch comparison
sections.html:
Use show spanning-tree summary plus show spanning-tree vlan 1 and relevant interface/running configuration to confirm mode, intended C1 root, applied guards and feature status. The summary alone may not display every per-interface guard on every image, so inspect actual port detail as necessary. Screenshot C1, one distribution and one access switch. Repeat the same uplink disconnect/reconnect test after hardening and screenshot recovered pings: security controls must preserve legitimate failover.

A1 test: temporarily replace PC1’s connection at A1 Fa0/1 with the additional course-lab switch, so the port receives BPDUs. Run show interfaces status and show interfaces fastEthernet 0/1. Expect err-disabled due to Guard; capture actual output. Remove the switch, reconnect PC1, then reset the interface with shutdown followed by no shutdown inside interface configuration. Do not re-enable while the triggering device remains attached.

A2 comparison: attach that same extra switch to A2 Fa0/1. With the explicit interface Filter command, expect the port to remain up while BPDUs are ignored; capture status and remove the extra switch. This demonstrates silent filtering, not proof of safe operation with redundant physical paths. Record observations rather than manufacturing them.

Reflection: rapid convergence principally improves day-to-day availability after a fault; edge Guard principally contains unauthorized topology participation and reveals a policy violation. Reliability and security overlap in availability but are not identical. Prefer Guard on typical corporate PC ports for visible containment and investigate false positives; keep Filter for carefully justified special cases.

tutorialAnswers.question: Q1. Explain why STP is necessary in a network with redundant switch links, and what would actually happen to that network without it.   [LO1]
tutorialAnswers.answerHtml: Model revision answer. Redundant switch links provide backup paths but can form active Layer 2 loops. Ethernet frames lack an IP-style hop limit, so broadcasts and unknown traffic can circulate/replicate, causing storms, duplicate frames and repeated MAC-table moves. STP exchanges BPDUs, elects a root and logically blocks selected redundant ports to preserve one active tree. Physical links remain available for activation after a failure.

tutorialAnswers.question: Q2. Describe the three steps of the STP algorithm (root bridge election, root port election, designated port election), and explain what determines the outcome of each step.   [LO1]
tutorialAnswers.answerHtml: Model revision answer. First elect the lowest Bridge ID root: configured priority first, then MAC/system-ID details as relevant. Second, each non-root selects the port with lowest cumulative cost to that root; equal-cost paths are resolved by BPDU bridge/port tie-breakers. Third, each segment selects its designated port using the best advertised root/path information; remaining redundant ports block/discard. A root port is chosen per non-root switch, while a designated port is chosen per segment, so those roles must not be conflated.

tutorialAnswers.question: Q3. A switch has two possible paths back to the root bridge: a direct 100 Mbps link (cost 19), and an indirect path through a neighbouring switch that costs 4 to reach the root plus a further 19 to reach this switch. Calculate the Root Path Cost of each option, state which becomes this switch's Root Port, and explain your reasoning.   [LO1]
tutorialAnswers.answerHtml: Model revision answer. The direct 100 Mbps link has cost 19. The indirect option adds the neighbor’s root cost 4 and the link to that neighbor 19, totaling 23. The port on the direct path becomes the root port because 19 is lower than 23. Count all links toward the root once; do not compare only the last link speed or assume the route with a faster single link is always best.

tutorialAnswers.question: Q4. Describe the four STP port states in order, and explain why RSTP's new port roles allow it to reach a forwarding state far faster than classic STP.   [LO1]
tutorialAnswers.answerHtml: Model revision answer. The requested classic sequence is Blocking → Listening → Learning → Forwarding. Blocking/listening do not forward user data or learn MACs; learning populates forwarding entries without forwarding user data; forwarding does both. RSTP adds alternate and backup roles and rapid agreement behavior so a valid standby path can take over without waiting all classic timers under suitable conditions. It still preserves loop-safety checks; not every topology/failure is guaranteed instantaneous.

tutorialAnswers.question: Q5. Compare STP, RSTP, PVST+/Rapid PVST+, and MSTP. What does each version add over the one before it?   [LO1]
tutorialAnswers.answerHtml: Model revision answer. STP/802.1D provides the original loop-free single-tree function with slow timer-driven recovery. RSTP/802.1w adds rapid transitions, defined alternate/backup roles and handshake behavior. Cisco PVST+ applies a classic tree per VLAN, and Rapid PVST+ combines per-VLAN trees with rapid behavior, permitting different VLANs to favor different redundant links. MSTP/802.1s groups many VLANs into fewer instances to reduce instance overhead. These are related protocol families, not a perfectly linear ladder in which every version replaces all others. The supplied Packet Tracer lab uses PVST+ and Rapid PVST+; it says MSTP is unavailable there.

tutorialAnswers.question: Q6. Describe how the STP root bridge manipulation attack works, and explain why the lack of authentication on BPDUs is what makes it possible.   [LO1]
tutorialAnswers.answerHtml: Model revision answer. The attacker sends BPDUs advertising a superior Bridge ID, typically a lower priority than the intended root. Because ordinary BPDUs do not prove authorization, switches accept the claimed better root and recalculate the tree. Depending on the physical transit position, this can redirect paths for interception or cause instability/DoS. Becoming root alone with one edge connection does not guarantee every data frame crosses the attacker. Guard host ports against BPDUs and reject superior downstream claims with Root Guard.

tutorialAnswers.question: Q7. Explain how Topology Change (TC) Flooding/Spoofing degrades network performance. What concept from Week 3 does the resulting symptom resemble, and why?   [LO1]
tutorialAnswers.answerHtml: Model revision answer. TC flooding sends repeated false topology-change notifications or repeatedly changes port state, causing accelerated aging/invalidation and relearning of MAC entries. Unknown destinations then flood more often, consuming capacity and potentially exposing traffic. This resembles Week 3 CAM flooding in its unknown-unicast symptom, but TC flooding repeatedly invalidates information while CAM flooding consumes the table with invented sources. The attacker need not win root election.

tutorialAnswers.question: Q8. Explain how an attacker can cause a network-wide denial of service using STP without ever becoming the root bridge.   [LO1]
tutorialAnswers.answerHtml: Model revision answer. A BPDU flood can consume switch control-plane processing and induce repeated tree calculations through changing root/path claims. Fabricated TCNs also force persistent relearning. Availability can degrade across the switched network even if the current root remains unchanged; exhausting processing or creating instability is a different goal from becoming root. Edge BPDU Guard can contain a source arriving on a forbidden host port, but legitimate infrastructure links still require appropriate monitoring/control-plane protection.

tutorialAnswers.question: Q9. For each of Root Guard, BPDU Guard, and Loop Guard, state which of this week's three attacks it would actually prevent, and explain your reasoning for each.   [LO2]
tutorialAnswers.answerHtml: Model revision answer. Root Guard prevents superior downstream root claims on designated ports, directly addressing root manipulation; it does not reject arbitrary TC messages or every flood. BPDU Guard stops all three patterns when their BPDUs enter through a protected end-device port because any BPDU err-disables that port; it cannot be applied indiscriminately to real inter-switch ports. Loop Guard addresses unexpected loss of expected BPDUs and loop risk from failures. It is not a direct defense against any of the three fabricated-message attacks as generally defined, although it is a useful complementary availability safeguard.

tutorialAnswers.question: Q10. BPDU Guard and BPDU Filter protect the same PC-facing access ports, but respond to an incoming BPDU completely differently. Describe that difference, and evaluate which one you would recommend for a corporate office's PC ports, justifying your choice.   [LO1, LO2]
tutorialAnswers.answerHtml: Model revision answer. BPDU Guard treats any BPDU as a violation and puts the host port into err-disabled state, giving visible containment requiring investigation/recovery. The lab’s interface-level BPDU Filter silently discards BPDUs and leaves the port forwarding, so the rogue control claim is ignored without a Guard-style shutdown. Recommend Guard for normal corporate PC ports: it enforces the end-host assumption and reveals violation. Unconditional filtering also removes STP protection on that interface and can permit loops if another path is introduced, so its apparent uptime is not equivalent protection. Global default filtering behaves differently from explicit interface filtering.

tutorialAnswers.question: Q11. Explain the difference between what BackboneFast and UplinkFast each optimise for, and why a network might reasonably need both rather than just one.   [LO2]
tutorialAnswers.answerHtml: Model revision answer. BackboneFast optimizes classic-STP recovery from indirect failures elsewhere in the backbone, reducing waiting for old root information to expire. UplinkFast optimizes direct failure of an access switch’s current root uplink by bringing a standby uplink into use quickly. A classic hierarchical design can encounter both failure types, so the features address different cases. RSTP/Rapid PVST+ incorporates fast-convergence behavior, so these legacy options should not be described as essential extra acceleration in every rapid network.

tutorialAnswers.question: Q12. A network administrator has configured BPDU Guard on every access port, but has not touched the distribution or core switches at all. Evaluate this configuration: which attacks does it stop, and what STP-related risk remains unaddressed?   [LO2, LO3]
tutorialAnswers.answerHtml: Model revision answer. BPDU Guard on all genuine host ports blocks root claims, false TCs and BPDU floods entering through those ports by disabling the source port. That is a strong edge layer, but trusted inter-switch paths can still receive superior claims from a misconfigured/compromised infrastructure switch, and missing BPDUs on redundant links can create unsafe transitions. Set intended root priority, place Root Guard on appropriate downstream designated ports, and use Loop Guard on suitable root/alternate links. Rapid convergence and monitoring improve reliability/visibility but do not authenticate every legitimate infrastructure message.

tutorialAnswers.question: Part 1, Step 1.1: build and configure all trunk/access links
tutorialAnswers.answerHtml: Model lab answer / expected method. Build C1↔D1/D2, D1↔D2, D1/D2↔A1/A2, PC1↔A1 and PC2↔A2 using the exact port plan in the lab section. C1 Gi0/1–2 are trunks. D1/D2 Gi0/1–2 and Fa0/1–2 are trunks. A1/A2 Gi0/1–2 are trunks and Fa0/1 is access. The full device-group configuration is provided in the lab notes above. Confirm physical links and trunk roles before continuing.

tutorialAnswers.question: Part 1, Step 1.2: address the PCs
tutorialAnswers.answerHtml: Model lab answer / expected method. Use PC1 192.168.1.10/24 and PC2 192.168.1.20/24 with mask 255.255.255.0. Both are in 192.168.1.0/24 and VLAN 1, so they can communicate through switching without inter-VLAN routing or a default gateway. Check for duplicate addresses and allow initial STP/ARP convergence before diagnosing a failed first ping.

tutorialAnswers.question: Part 1, Step 2: identify the default root, blocked ports and backbone designated port
tutorialAnswers.answerHtml: Model lab answer / expected method. Run show spanning-tree vlan 1 on all five switches. Record the actual Root ID and which local Bridge ID matches it; do not infer a name. If priorities are equal, lowest MAC determines root. List the actual blocking/discarding ports and explain how each closes a redundant loop. On D1/D2 Gi0/2, compare advertised root costs; lower cost wins designated, with Bridge ID breaking an equal-cost tie. The initial answer depends on the observed root and costs, so no single named port/root can be supplied without output. Capture at least two real outputs showing a root and blocked port.

tutorialAnswers.question: Part 1, Step 3: measure baseline PVST+ convergence
tutorialAnswers.answerHtml: Model lab answer / expected method. Ping PC2 from PC1 repeatedly, disconnect the selected A1 uplink, and record loss count plus elapsed recovery time; reconnect and stabilize. The guide suggests roughly 30–50 seconds for classic behavior, but that is an expected range, not a result to copy. Report the chosen failed link, ping interval, observed failures and actual elapsed time. A failed standby link may not interrupt the flow, so note the selected port role when interpreting the test.

tutorialAnswers.question: Part 1, Step 4: Rapid PVST+ comparison
tutorialAnswers.answerHtml: Model lab answer / expected method. Set spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst on every switch. Repeat the same A1-link failure/reconnection with the same timing method and record actual recovery. Compare the measured rapid result with the measured baseline and explain faster standby transitions/handshake behavior. Keep Rapid PVST+ for Part 2. The lab’s Packet Tracer environment does not provide standalone IEEE RSTP or MSTP configuration modes.

tutorialAnswers.question: Part 2, Step 2.1: choose C1 deterministically
tutorialAnswers.answerHtml: Model lab answer / expected method. On C1 use spanning-tree vlan 1 priority 4096 and verify that its Root ID matches its Bridge ID on VLAN 1. It should defeat the other default base-priority 32768 switches. VLAN-extended output may show 4097 for VLAN 1. A rogue with an even lower ID could still win where unguarded; configured priority is a topology choice, not authentication.

tutorialAnswers.question: Part 2, Step 2.2: deploy Root Guard
tutorialAnswers.answerHtml: Model lab answer / expected method. On both D1 and D2 enter interface range fastEthernet 0/1 - 2 and spanning-tree guard root. These are downstream designated ports toward A1/A2 that should not become root paths. A superior claim from that direction is rejected through root-inconsistent non-forwarding state instead of replacing C1. Do not put this setting on an uplink that legitimately needs to be a root port.

tutorialAnswers.question: Part 2, Steps 2.3–2.4: different edge protections
tutorialAnswers.answerHtml: Model lab answer / expected method. A1 Fa0/1 receives spanning-tree portfast plus spanning-tree bpduguard enable. A2 Fa0/1 receives spanning-tree portfast plus spanning-tree bpdufilter enable for the isolated comparison. Guard responds to any received BPDU with err-disable. The explicit Filter suppresses BPDU participation but leaves data forwarding active, so its absence of shutdown must not be mistaken for equal loop protection. Full commands are in the notes.

tutorialAnswers.question: Part 2, Steps 2.5–2.6: redundant-uplink and backbone settings
tutorialAnswers.answerHtml: Model lab answer / expected method. On A1/A2 Gi0/1–2 apply spanning-tree guard loop, and at switch scope apply spanning-tree uplinkfast. On D1/D2 at switch scope apply spanning-tree backbonefast. Loop Guard prevents unsafe forwarding after expected BPDU loss; UplinkFast covers direct classic root-uplink failure; BackboneFast covers indirect classic failures. The guide explicitly says not to expect dramatic extra convergence improvement under Rapid PVST+; confirm command support/status rather than claiming unmeasured benefits.

tutorialAnswers.question: Part 2, Step 3: verify and screenshot configuration
tutorialAnswers.answerHtml: Model lab answer / expected method. Run show spanning-tree summary and show spanning-tree vlan 1. Confirm rapid mode, actual intended C1 root, and feature settings. Inspect port-specific spanning-tree details/running configuration where the simulator summary does not display per-port Root/Loop Guard. Capture actual outputs from C1, one distribution switch and one access switch. Configuration evidence and operational root/role evidence serve different purposes; keep both.

tutorialAnswers.question: Part 2, Step 4: verify legitimate connectivity and failover
tutorialAnswers.answerHtml: Model lab answer / expected method. Re-run the same A1-uplink interruption after all hardening. Record that PC1↔PC2 communication recovers, compare recovery with the earlier rapid test, reconnect and stabilize. Screenshot the successful recovered pings. If the test fails, inspect root/port roles, guard-induced states, trunk consistency and addressing; do not mark the task complete from command entry alone.

tutorialAnswers.question: Part 2, Step 5a: demonstrate A1 BPDU Guard and restore service
tutorialAnswers.answerHtml: Model lab answer / expected method. In the isolated topology, temporarily connect the additional lab switch to A1 Fa0/1 in place of PC1. Its BPDUs should trigger Guard, so show interfaces status and show interfaces fastEthernet 0/1 should reveal an err-disabled port. Capture actual evidence. Remove the extra switch, reconnect PC1, then in interface Fa0/1 configuration issue shutdown followed by no shutdown to recover. Confirm PC1 connectivity; resetting while the BPDU source remains attached would retrigger the violation.

tutorialAnswers.question: Part 2, Step 5b and Step 6: demonstrate A2 Filter and compare
tutorialAnswers.answerHtml: Model lab answer / expected method. Move the same temporary switch to A2 Fa0/1. With explicit interface BPDU Filter, show interfaces status and the interface detail should show the link up rather than Guard’s err-disabled response while BPDUs are ignored. Capture actual output and remove the temporary switch. Comparison: A1 visibly contained unauthorized BPDU participation; A2 silently retained link availability and provided no equivalent violation response. The test has one temporary connection; a redundant path with unconditional Filter can produce a loop.

tutorialAnswers.question: Final reflection: security posture versus daily reliability
tutorialAnswers.answerHtml: Model lab answer / expected method. Model reflection: My actual baseline and Rapid PVST+ measurements show how fast the network restores service after the tested failure; I would insert the measured numbers rather than copy the guide’s range. Rapid convergence mainly improves operational availability, while BPDU Guard’s shutdown demonstrates enforcement of the no-switch-on-PC-port rule. Security and reliability overlap, but fast failover does not authenticate BPDUs and silent uptime does not establish safe topology control. I would choose BPDU Guard for ordinary corporate PC ports because unexpected BPDUs trigger visible containment and investigation. Unconditional BPDU Filter may conceal unauthorized participation and removes loop protection at that interface, so it needs a specific justified use rather than being the default.

sections.title: How routers learn and compare routes
sections.html:
A router forwards using its routing table. Dynamic routing exchanges reachability information automatically, replacing manual maintenance at scale. Security depends on which neighbours and claims the router accepts. An attractive route changes the next hop; the attacker may then drop, inspect or relay traffic.

ProtocolType and metricTransportMessages and trust
RIPDistance-vector; fewest hops, maximum reachable 15; 16 = unreachableUDP 520; RIPv1 broadcast, RIPv2 224.0.0.9Request and Response; full updates normally every 30 s. RIPv1 no authentication; RIPv2 optional cleartext/MD5.
OSPFLink-state; cost = reference bandwidth/interface bandwidth, summed along path; topology database per area, Area 0 backboneIP protocol 89; 224.0.0.5 all OSPF routers; 224.0.0.6 DR/BDRHello, DBD, LSR, LSU, LSAck; MD5 protects neighbour exchanges in lecture/lab.
EIGRPAdvanced distance-vector, DUAL; bandwidth and delay by default; load/reliability available but normally disabledIP protocol 88; 224.0.0.10Hello, Update, Query, Reply, Acknowledgment; Query/Reply supports loop-free convergence.
BGPPath-vector between Autonomous Systems; ordered attributes such as weight, local preference, AS path and originTCP 179OPEN, UPDATE, KEEPALIVE, NOTIFICATION. Session MD5 is carried as a TCP option.

OSPF example: with reference bandwidth 100 Mb/s, a 10 Mb/s interface has cost 10 and a 100 Mb/s interface cost 1. Actual configured reference bandwidth matters. RIP treats either link as one hop. BGP is policy driven; shorter AS path is only one selection factor, not its sole metric.

sections.title: Five routing attacks: cause, action and consequence
sections.html:
AttackVulnerability and techniqueImpactControls
Routing table poisoningFalse advertisements with attractive metrics: RIP Response, EIGRP Update, OSPF rogue LSA or BGP UPDATE analogueWrong next hop, interception and/or DoSNeighbour authentication, route filtering, passive access interfaces
Unauthorised route injectionRogue device becomes a continuing routing participant. OSPF/EIGRP form Hello-based adjacencies; RIP may accept an injected Response without adjacency; BGP normally requires a configured peer/sessionPersistent false routes plus topology visibilityAuthentication, passive-interface, physical port controls
BGP route/prefix hijackingAnnounce an unauthorised IP prefix, often more specific than the real routeInternet-scale redirection, interception or outageProvider prefix filters and RPKI origin validation
Blackhole / sinkholeUse poisoning/injection/hijacking to redirect to a discard path or an attacker-controlled receiverBlackhole = dropped traffic/DoS; sinkhole = collection, possible tampering and optional forwardingPrevent route manipulation; monitor path changes, drops and latency
Routing DoS / instabilityFlood updates or repeatedly announce/withdraw routes; trigger SPF, DUAL or BGP recomputationCPU exhaustion, unstable forwarding and loss of availabilityAuthentication, control-plane limits, careful route dampening

These are not mutually exclusive labels. Poisoning describes how routing information is falsified; blackhole/sinkhole describes what subsequently happens to the traffic. A legitimate but compromised neighbour can conduct either.

sections.title: Case study: YouTube, 24 February 2008
sections.html:
Pakistan Telecom (AS17557) tried to block YouTube domestically by announcing 208.65.153.0/24, a more-specific part of YouTube's 208.65.152.0/22. Its upstream PCCW (AS3491) propagated the announcement globally instead of confining/filtering it. Longest-prefix matching drew traffic towards Pakistan Telecom and produced an outage of roughly two hours. This illustrates how a local configuration decision can become a global incident.

A /22 includes four /24 networks; a destination within 208.65.153.0/24 matches both announcements and follows the /24. Provider filtering should accept only prefixes authorised for that customer. A correct ROA plus configured rejection of Invalid announcements would reject the unauthorised origin.

sections.title: Authentication, passive interfaces and route filters
sections.html:
Shared-key neighbour authentication prevents a device lacking the key from becoming a trusted routing peer or submitting accepted authenticated updates. It does not encrypt the topology, verify the physical existence of a route, or protect against a compromised authorised neighbour. The MD5 examples are the legacy lab mechanism; use modern supported authentication in production.

ControlOSPFEIGRP
MD5 configurationEnable message-digest authentication per area or interface; set interface message-digest key. The lecture contrasts a simple active-key arrangement with EIGRP key chains.Define a named key chain, key ID and secret; apply MD5 mode and the key chain to the interface. Key lifetimes support planned rotation.
Passive-interfaceSuppresses Hellos/adjacency on user-facing links while the network can still be advertised through other active interfaces.Suppresses Hellos/adjacency on user-facing links; network still advertised through active neighbours.
Distribute-listNormally filters routes entering the local routing table; cannot simply stop intra-area LSA propagation because routers need a consistent LSDB. Area-boundary tools are different.Can filter routes in Update exchange, affecting route propagation.

Filter even authenticated neighbours: authentication controls who can speak; filtering controls what may be learned/advertised. For BGP, apply customer-specific prefix allowlists at provider boundaries. Use passive-interface only where no neighbour is required; RIP receiving behaviour differs from OSPF/EIGRP.

OSPF key-rotation qualification: the lecture's “one active key/no rotation out of the box” contrast is simplified. Cisco IOS documents multiple MD5 key IDs and rollover that sends authenticated copies during migration. EIGRP key-chain lifetimes are still the lab distinction, but OSPF is not universally incapable of rollover. See Cisco OSPF message-digest-key command reference. For passive interfaces, Cisco EIGRP passive-interface explanation confirms that EIGRP suppresses adjacency whereas RIP commonly still receives updates.

sections.title: RPKI and Route Origin Authorisations
sections.html:
A Regional Internet Registry (RIPE NCC, ARIN or APNIC, for example) provides a resource certificate binding address resources to a holder. The holder publishes a signed ROA specifying a prefix, authorised origin AS and maximum permitted prefix length. Validators download and verify the certificate/ROA chain; routers use validated results in policy.

ResultMeaningPolicy consequence
ValidAt least one covering ROA authorises the origin AS and advertised prefix length.Normally eligible for ordinary BGP policy; not proof of the entire path.
InvalidCovering ROA data exists, but no ROA authorises both origin and length.Configure rejection; an incorrect legitimate ROA can also produce Invalid.
NotFoundNo covering ROA exists.Unvalidated, commonly still eligible; not synonymous with malicious.

Origin validation does not check every AS hop and works only when resources have ROAs and operators use the results. The lecture table's “Invalid → rejected” describes intended filtering policy, not an automatic property of validation. See RFC 6811, BGP Prefix Origin Validation.

sections.title: Layered recommendation and exam reasoning
sections.html:
For an internal routing domain: authenticate router-facing links, make end-user interfaces passive, restrict physical access and filter plausible prefixes. Add control-plane rate limits and monitoring for churn or path changes. For external BGP: filter customer prefixes and apply RPKI validation policy. Dampening can suppress repeatedly flapping routes but needs careful tuning because legitimate instability may also be penalised.

Packet Tracer scope: OSPF and EIGRP MD5 are the two reliable lab targets in these supplied lectures. RIPv2 authentication varies by simulator version and BGP support is limited. This is a tool-support limitation, not evidence that RIP/BGP cannot be authenticated in real networks.

quiz.question: A RIPv2 route is advertised at metric 16. How is it treated?
quiz.explanation: RIP accepts at most 15 reachable hops; 16 denotes unreachable.

quiz.question: Which routing packet runs directly over IP protocol 89?
quiz.explanation: OSPF uses IP protocol 89; EIGRP uses 88, RIP UDP 520 and BGP TCP 179.

quiz.question: An authenticated neighbour advertises a prohibited prefix. Which control directly restricts the content of that claim?
quiz.explanation: Authentication proves key possession; filtering limits accepted or advertised prefixes.

quiz.question: Why did the YouTube /24 divert destinations also covered by its legitimate /22?
options: Longest-prefix matching selects the more-specific route
AS17557 had the smallest AS number
quiz.explanation: The destination matches both routes; the /24 is more specific.

quiz.question: What is a plain OSPF distribute-list normally able to change?
quiz.explanation: Intra-area LSA flooding remains; boundary filtering uses other mechanisms.

quiz.question: A covering ROA authorises AS100 with maxLength /24. AS100 announces a /25. Result?
options: Always accepted because the AS matches
quiz.explanation: Origin and length must both be authorised; /25 exceeds the permitted /24 maximum.

quiz.question: Which attack primarily keeps the control plane recalculating rather than selecting one malicious next hop?
quiz.explanation: Repeated announcements/withdrawals or update floods consume control-plane resources.

quiz.question: Which statement about lab authentication is best supported?
options: Packet Tracer supports every BGP feature
OSPF and EIGRP are the reliable supplied lab targets
RPKI is an OSPF key chain
quiz.explanation: The lecture explicitly scopes reliable Packet Tracer MD5 practice to OSPF/EIGRP.

tutorialAnswers.question: Q1. Compare RIP, OSPF, EIGRP, and BGP by type (distance-vector, link-state, advanced distance-vector, or path-vector) and by the metric each one uses to select a best path.   [LO1]
tutorialAnswers.answerHtml:
ProtocolTypeBest-path metric
RIPDistance-vectorHop count; maximum 15
OSPFLink-stateSummed bandwidth-derived cost; topology per area
EIGRPAdvanced distance-vectorComposite bandwidth and delay by default; DUAL convergence
BGPPath-vectorOrdered attributes, including local preference and AS-path length; policy driven

tutorialAnswers.question: Q2. Describe the message types OSPF uses to form and maintain a neighbor relationship, and explain which specific message type MD5 authentication actually has to protect.   [LO1]
tutorialAnswers.answerHtml: Hello discovers/maintains neighbours; DBD summarises the LSDB; LSR requests missing detail; LSU carries LSAs; LSAck acknowledges delivery. Authentication must protect Hello before adjacency is accepted, and it also authenticates the routing exchanges rather than protecting Hello alone.

tutorialAnswers.question: Q3. Explain why BGP's transport (TCP, port 179) is fundamentally different from the other three protocols covered this week, and what that difference means for how BGP's own authentication actually works.   [LO1]
tutorialAnswers.answerHtml: BGP uses a stateful TCP connection on port 179. RIP uses UDP 520; OSPF and EIGRP run directly over IP protocols 89 and 88. The lecture's BGP MD5 mechanism is a TCP-header option authenticating the session's TCP segments, not an OSPF/EIGRP-style routing-protocol field. It does not prove prefix ownership.

tutorialAnswers.question: Q4. Explain how Routing Table Poisoning works, and describe how the exact technique differs between a distance-vector protocol like RIP and a link-state protocol like OSPF.   [LO1]
tutorialAnswers.answerHtml: An attacker supplies a false attractive route and legitimate routers select/propagate it. RIP accepts neighbour distance claims, so a forged Response claiming a low hop count can poison reachability. OSPF uses a topology database, so the analogue is forged/rogue LSAs altering advertised links or reachability and causing SPF recalculation. OSPF is not a distance-vector protocol, even though false routing information can poison its resulting table.

tutorialAnswers.question: Q5. Distinguish Unauthorised Route Injection from Routing Table Poisoning. What does the attacker actually gain in each case that's different from the other?   [LO1]
tutorialAnswers.answerHtml: Poisoning focuses on incorrect information entering routing decisions; it need not establish a persistent adjacency, especially with RIP. Unauthorised injection focuses on a rogue continuing routing participant: it can learn topology and keep submitting updates. One rogue participant can repeatedly perform poisoning, so the attacks overlap.

tutorialAnswers.question: Q6. Explain why Route/Prefix Hijacking is considered a BGP-specific attack, using the 2008 YouTube hijack to illustrate your answer.   [LO1, LO3]
tutorialAnswers.answerHtml: Internet prefix ownership/origination is communicated between ASes through BGP. In 2008 AS17557 announced YouTube's 208.65.153.0/24 inside the legitimate 208.65.152.0/22, and AS3491 propagated it. The more-specific route attracted global traffic, causing an approximately two-hour outage. Internal protocols can misroute local reachability, but do not provide this inter-AS origin-claim role.

tutorialAnswers.question: Q7. Explain the difference between a blackhole outcome and a sinkhole outcome, and why both share the same underlying vulnerability as the injection and poisoning attacks.   [LO1]
tutorialAnswers.answerHtml: Blackhole means diverted traffic is dropped; sinkhole means it reaches a controlled receiver that can inspect, alter or optionally forward it. Both rely on accepting manipulated next-hop information, commonly through poisoning or rogue route injection. Their distinction is the outcome after misdirection.

tutorialAnswers.question: Q8. A network administrator asks you which single defense would do the most to reduce risk across this week's five attacks. Evaluate neighbor authentication (MD5) against this question, including what it does not protect against.   [LO2]
tutorialAnswers.answerHtml: Neighbour authentication is the strongest single broad control here: it rejects updates from devices without the shared key and reduces poisoning, rogue participation, blackhole/sinkhole setup and update flooding. It neither proves an authenticated advertisement true nor validates BGP origin ownership; compromised peers, key theft and volume still require filtering, passive interfaces, control-plane protection, monitoring and RPKI for BGP.

tutorialAnswers.question: Q9. Explain why this week's lab only covers OSPF and EIGRP authentication, not all four protocols covered in the lecture.   [LO2]
tutorialAnswers.answerHtml: The supplied lab chooses protocols with reliable MD5 implementation in Packet Tracer: OSPF and EIGRP. RIPv2 support varies with Packet Tracer version and BGP support is limited. RIP and BGP remain examinable theory; the simulator restriction is not a general protocol restriction.

tutorialAnswers.question: Q10. Compare how MD5 authentication is actually configured on OSPF versus EIGRP, and explain the practical trade-off between the two approaches.   [LO2]
tutorialAnswers.answerHtml:
OSPF enables message-digest authentication per area or interface and places a message-digest key on the interface. EIGRP first defines a key chain and keys, then applies authentication mode MD5 and that chain to the interface. The lecture contrasts OSPF's simpler active-key setup with EIGRP's extra setup that enables multiple keys/lifetimes and planned rotation. Match keys/mode on both peers and verify adjacency.

Qualification: Cisco IOS also supports OSPF MD5 key rollover with multiple key IDs, so do not claim OSPF can never rotate without downtime. The tutorial comparison describes the supplied simplified configuration model.

tutorialAnswers.question: Q11. A colleague says: ‘We've applied a distribute-list on our OSPF network, so we're now confident no unauthorised route can propagate to other routers.’ Evaluate this claim. Is it accurate? Why or why not?   [LO2]
tutorialAnswers.answerHtml: The claim is inaccurate. OSPF routers in an area must share a consistent LSDB; an ordinary distribute-list limits which routes enter this router's routing table, not which LSAs flood to peers. Therefore other routers can still receive the information. Use suitable area-boundary filtering where applicable, plus authentication and a design suited to the required control.

tutorialAnswers.question: Q12. Explain what RPKI does, and why it directly addresses the specific weakness that caused the 2008 YouTube hijack.   [LO1, LO2]
tutorialAnswers.answerHtml: RPKI binds resource holders to address space using a certificate hierarchy; the holder signs a ROA authorising an origin AS and maximum prefix length. Origin validation would flag AS17557's YouTube origin as Invalid if a covering ROA authorised the real origin (lecture example AS36561), and an upstream configured to reject Invalid announcements would stop its propagation. It does not validate the full AS path, and NotFound means no covering ROA rather than proven legitimacy.

sections.title: Transport duties, TCP guarantees and sockets
sections.html:
Layer 4 delivers between processes: port-based multiplexing/demultiplexing identifies applications on a host, transport units carry application data, and checksums detect transmission errors. The lecture lists segmentation, multiplexing, demultiplexing, process-to-process delivery and error detection as common tasks. UDP preserves application datagrams rather than segmenting/reassembling a reliable byte stream; applications must respect message-size limits.

FunctionTCPUDP
Setup/stateThree-way handshake; statefulNo handshake or protocol connection state
Reliability/orderAcknowledgements, retransmissions and sequence-ordered byte delivery while connection operatesBest-effort datagrams; no delivery or order guarantee
Flow controlReceiver window protects receiver capacityNone built into UDP
Congestion controlAdjusts sending rate for path congestionNone built into UDP; responsible applications implement suitable control
Header20 bytes minimum8 bytes
Typical usesWeb, email, file transferDNS, VoIP, games, live media; some modern applications add reliability above UDP

A socket endpoint is an IP address plus port. A TCP connection is identified by source IP/port and destination IP/port (with protocol distinguishing transport namespaces). Many connections to one web server coexist because source endpoints differ. It is not required that every browser tab have its own TCP connection; tabs may share connections.

Checksum qualification: IPv4 UDP can use a zero checksum; IPv6 ordinarily requires one, with specific tunnel exceptions. A checksum is not a MAC. See RFC 8095, transport services.

sections.title: Handshake resources and orderly close
sections.html:
Client → Server: SYN, seq=x
Server → Client: SYN-ACK, seq=y, ack=x+1
Client → Server: ACK, seq=x+1, ack=y+1

A conventional server receiving SYN allocates a half-open backlog entry/Transmission Control Block before it knows the source is reachable. It sends SYN-ACK and waits for final ACK or timeout. On completion, it becomes established and obtains the buffers/resources needed for data transfer. Exact allocation varies by operating system and SYN-cookie use; the examinable asymmetry is state allocated before return-path verification.

Active closer → Peer: FIN
Peer → Active closer: ACK
Peer → Active closer: FIN (when its own sending is finished)
Active closer → Peer: ACK; enters TIME_WAIT

FIN closes one sending direction, so the peer may still send data before its FIN. ACK and FIN can combine. The active closer holds TIME_WAIT state to handle delayed duplicates and retransmit a final ACK when needed; traditional duration is twice maximum segment lifetime, with implementation-specific timing. Rapid connection churn can consume tuple/state resources even after application data has ended.

sections.title: TCP reconnaissance: ports, hosts and OS
sections.html:
AttackProbe and interpretationValue to attackerDefence
TCP port scanSYN to many ports on one host: SYN-ACK suggests open, RST closed; silence/ICMP may indicate filtering. SYN scan avoids completing the connection; connect scan completes it.Find listening services for later attacksDisable unnecessary services; consistent filtering; detect vertical scans; rate-limit
FIN / Xmas / NULL scanFIN only; FIN+PSH+URG; no flags. Some stacks RST closed ports but silently drop probes at open ports; firewalls/OS differ.May evade simplistic SYN-only rules; open-or-filtered ambiguityStateful validation and scan detection; do not rely only on SYN flag signatures
TCP host sweepProbe one common port across many IP addresses; either SYN-ACK or RST proves a responding host.Discover live addresses despite blocked ICMP echoDetect horizontal scan patterns; segmentation; minimise exposure
OS fingerprintingCompare TTL, TCP windows/options and responses to unusual packets with known patterns.Choose likely OS/version-specific vulnerabilitiesPatch; optional stack normalisation; defence in depth

Reconnaissance is not itself successful compromise. SYN scans remain visible to network monitoring even without a completed application connection. No response does not uniquely identify host/port state.

sections.title: TCP hijacking, reset injection and SYN floods
sections.html:
AttackMechanism and outcomeDefence and limitations
TCP hijackingSpoof established flow identifiers and acceptable sequence numbers to inject data as a peer. On-path capture can reveal numbers; historical predictable ISNs made blind injection easier.TLS record authentication rejects forged content. Random ISNs reduce off-path guessing; monitor abnormal sequence/ACK behaviour.
TCP RST injectionForge an acceptable reset for a live flow to terminate it; disruption rather than content takeover.Random ISNs and stronger TCP reset validation make blind attacks harder; monitor resets and reconnect where appropriate. TLS does not authenticate RST.
TCP SYN floodMany SYNs without final ACK fill half-open backlog faster than timeout releases it, often with spoofed sources. New clients cannot connect.SYN cookies encode recoverable state in SYN-ACK sequence values until ACK returns. Backlog/timeout tuning only increases tolerance. SYN-rate filtering and upstream DDoS mitigation address remaining processing/link limits.

RST qualification: the lecture describes the older “in-window reset” model. RFC 5961 strengthens it: an exact expected sequence can reset; an in-window non-exact value triggers a challenge ACK. See RFC 5961. TLS cannot stop an otherwise acceptable forged TCP reset because TCP headers are outside its record authentication. IPsec or TCP-level authentication may protect that layer when correctly deployed.

sections.title: UDP: four attacks from a minimal protocol
sections.html:
UDP sends immediately, without setup, retransmission, ordering, receiver flow control or built-in congestion control. A high-rate sender can cheaply generate traffic and spoof source addresses unless the network filters them. The victim still spends bandwidth, processing and sometimes ICMP response work.

AttackMechanism / responseMitigation
UDP port scanMany ports on one host. ICMP Port Unreachable normally indicates closed; a service-specific reply indicates open; silence may mean open, filtered, loss or response throttling.Minimise exposed UDP services; detect scans; rate-limit ICMP responses while preserving necessary network functions.
UDP host sweepProbe one service across many IPs; application replies or ICMP errors reveal live hosts even when ICMP echo is blocked.Horizontal scan detection, segmentation, exposure reduction and rate limits.
UDP bombMalformed length/header relationships crash a vulnerable stack; a legacy implementation defect, not inherent to every UDP receiver.Patch OS/firmware, validate packets at firewall/IPS; pay attention to long-lived embedded systems.
UDP floodHigh packet volume consumes bandwidth/CPU; closed-port ICMP generation can add extra work.Filter unnecessary ports, rate-limit UDP/ICMP, filter spoofed sources; upstream protection for link-saturating floods.

DNS, NTP or memcached amplification combines UDP source spoofing with an application that sends a larger response to a spoofed victim address. This is application-protocol amplification on UDP, not UDP automatically multiplying packets.

sections.title: Proportionate layered mitigation
sections.html:
Start with configuration controls: remove unused services, enable SYN cookies where supported, patch stacks and filter spoofed sources at network boundaries. Add firewall/IDS scan detection and sensible per-source or aggregate rate limits. Segment hosts to reduce what a compromised machine can discover. Use authenticated encryption for application content and protect critical transport/control traffic at appropriate layers. Add dedicated upstream DDoS capacity where availability risk justifies it.

ICMP echo blocking alone cannot stop TCP/UDP sweeps. Blocking all ICMP can also interfere with legitimate error reporting and path diagnostics. An on-site firewall cannot recover bandwidth already saturated upstream. For exam answers, identify which resource is exhausted: SYN backlog, connection state, CPU, response generation or incoming link capacity.

quiz.question: A server receives SYN but never gets the final ACK. Which resource is the classic target?
quiz.explanation: A conventional SYN-RECEIVED entry holds resources until completion or timeout.

quiz.question: A SYN probe receives RST. Best interpretation?
options: The target port is closed and a responding host exists
quiz.explanation: RST is the normal closed-port TCP response and is also evidence of a live responder.

quiz.question: UDP probe receives no reply. What can safely be concluded?
options: Open or filtered/lost; more evidence needed
quiz.explanation: UDP has no handshake and silence is ambiguous.

quiz.question: Which control changes the SYN state-allocation asymmetry?
quiz.explanation: SYN cookies postpone stored half-open state until the final ACK validates the return path.

quiz.question: An attacker forges a valid TCP reset against a TLS session. What can occur?
options: TLS authenticates the RST and rejects it automatically
The TCP connection can terminate despite protected content
The attacker learns the TLS key automatically
RST becomes an encrypted HTTP request
quiz.explanation: TLS record integrity does not cover underlying TCP control headers.

quiz.question: One source probes destination port 80 on every IP in a subnet. This is primarily:
quiz.explanation: Host sweeps probe across hosts rather than many ports on one host.

quiz.question: Which attack relies on malformed UDP fields against a vulnerable parser?
quiz.explanation: UDP bomb targets header validation defects, commonly mitigated by patches and packet validation.

quiz.question: Why might a local firewall be insufficient during a huge UDP flood?
options: The upstream access link may already be saturated
quiz.explanation: Upstream absorption/filtering is needed when traffic volume exhausts the incoming link before local inspection.

tutorialAnswers.question: Q1. List Layer 4's mandatory tasks, common to both TCP and UDP, and then list what TCP adds on top of them. For each item TCP adds, explain in one sentence why UDP deliberately leaves it out.   [LO1]
tutorialAnswers.answerHtml: Shared duties in the lecture: segmentation/transport units, multiplexing, demultiplexing, process-to-process delivery and basic checksum error detection. TCP additionally establishes/terminates connections (UDP avoids setup latency), retransmits for reliability (UDP leaves loss handling to the application), orders bytes (UDP avoids waiting for missing data), controls receiver flow (UDP leaves pacing to the application), and controls congestion (UDP supplies no built-in algorithm). UDP datagrams are message oriented; it does not provide TCP-style reliable stream segmentation/reassembly. UDP is suitable where low delay or application-controlled recovery is preferred, not where correctness is unimportant.

tutorialAnswers.question: Q2. Explain what a socket is, and why the combination of source IP, source port, destination IP, and destination port matters more than the IP address alone.   [LO1]
tutorialAnswers.answerHtml: A socket endpoint combines IP address and port. The four TCP flow values distinguish simultaneous conversations between the same hosts and deliver each segment to its correct process/connection. One IP alone identifies a host, not which application or active conversation. Protocol also separates TCP from UDP namespaces.

tutorialAnswers.question: Q3. Describe the three-way handshake, and explain exactly what resource the server commits, and at which step, before it has any proof the client is genuine. Why does this detail matter for a later part of this worksheet?   [LO1]
tutorialAnswers.answerHtml: Client sends SYN with sequence x; server replies SYN-ACK with sequence y and ACK x+1; client sends ACK y+1. Conventionally the server allocates a half-open backlog/TCB entry on receiving SYN, before final ACK proves reachability. That finite pre-verification allocation is precisely what a SYN flood exhausts. SYN cookies are an exception that avoids keeping that half-open state.

tutorialAnswers.question: Q4. Describe how a TCP connection is torn down, and explain what the TIME_WAIT state is holding onto and why that could matter operationally, not just academically.   [LO1]
tutorialAnswers.answerHtml: One side sends FIN, peer ACKs, peer eventually sends its own FIN, and the active closer ACKs; the middle ACK/FIN can combine. Each FIN closes one sending direction. The active closer enters TIME_WAIT, retaining protocol/tuple state to handle delayed duplicates and a repeated FIN needing another ACK. Many rapid closes can accumulate TIME_WAIT entries and reduce available local ports/state; exact timing is OS dependent.

tutorialAnswers.question: Q5. Explain how a SYN scan differs from a full connect scan, and why an attacker might prefer one over the other.   [LO1]
tutorialAnswers.answerHtml: A SYN scan sends SYN and reads SYN-ACK/RST without completing a full connection, usually requiring raw-packet privileges; it can reduce application-level logging but remains visible to network sensors. A connect scan completes the OS TCP handshake and is typically easier without special privilege, but produces a full connection and more obvious logging. Both reveal service exposure.

tutorialAnswers.question: Q6. Explain why FIN, Xmas, and NULL scans can sometimes get past a firewall that a normal SYN scan would be caught by.   [LO1]
tutorialAnswers.answerHtml: A simplistic firewall that watches only new SYN attempts may overlook probes with FIN, FIN+PSH+URG (Xmas), or no flags (NULL). Some stacks RST closed ports but silently drop these probes at open ports, giving the scanner information. Results depend on OS/firewall behaviour, and silence remains open-or-filtered; stateful inspection and abnormal-flag detection reduce this gap.

tutorialAnswers.question: Q7. Explain what OS fingerprinting actually identifies, and why simply knowing a target's operating system is valuable to an attacker even before any vulnerability is confirmed.   [LO1]
tutorialAnswers.answerHtml: Fingerprinting estimates the operating system and sometimes version from TTLs, TCP window/options ordering and crafted-probe responses. It narrows the attacker's search to likely exploits/defaults and increases targeting efficiency. The identification alone is neither proof of a vulnerability nor a compromise; patching and layered controls still matter.

tutorialAnswers.question: Q8. TCP Hijacking and TCP RST Injection exploit almost exactly the same vulnerability. Explain what that shared vulnerability is, and then explain what actually distinguishes the two attacks from each other in terms of what the attacker is trying to achieve.   [LO1]
tutorialAnswers.answerHtml: Both exploit TCP's lack of cryptographic origin authentication for control/state, using spoofed flow identifiers and acceptable sequence numbers. Hijacking aims to inject attacker data or take over the session. RST injection aims to kill an existing flow with a reset. Random ISNs and modern reset validation hinder off-path guessing; TLS rejects injected content but cannot authenticate a TCP reset.

tutorialAnswers.question: Q9. Using what you learned about resource reservation during the handshake, explain step by step how a SYN flood actually exhausts a server, and why spoofed source addresses make the attack more effective rather than less.   [LO1]
tutorialAnswers.answerHtml: Attacker sends many SYNs; server allocates half-open entries and sends SYN-ACK; attacker never returns final ACK; entries survive until timeout; arrival rate exceeds expiry, so the backlog fills and new legitimate clients fail. Spoofed addresses hide/disperse sources and send SYN-ACKs to parties that did not request them, preventing intended completion. Valid established sessions may continue, though extreme network/CPU overload can affect everything.

tutorialAnswers.question: Q10. Evaluate SYN cookies as a mitigation. Why is this described as removing the vulnerability rather than just tolerating it, compared to simply increasing the backlog size?   [LO2]
tutorialAnswers.answerHtml: SYN cookies encode enough recoverable state in the SYN-ACK sequence number, so final ACK can be validated before normal connection state is allocated. This removes the particular stored half-open backlog asymmetry. A bigger backlog merely lets more fake entries coexist and still eventually fills. Cookies do not eliminate packet-processing costs or link-capacity limits, so rate limits and upstream DDoS measures may still be required.

tutorialAnswers.question: Q11. Explain why UDP port scanning is inherently harder and less reliable for an attacker than TCP port scanning, referencing what a UDP response (or lack of one) actually tells the scanner.   [LO1]
tutorialAnswers.answerHtml: TCP normally offers clear SYN-ACK/open and RST/closed responses. UDP has no handshake: ICMP Port Unreachable suggests closed, an application reply suggests open, and silence can mean open, firewall filtering, packet loss or ICMP throttling. A valid application-specific query such as DNS helps, but broad UDP scans remain slower and ambiguous.

tutorialAnswers.question: Q12. A network administrator argues that disabling ICMP entirely would stop most reconnaissance against their network. Evaluate this claim using at least two of today's attacks in your answer.   [LO2, LO3]
tutorialAnswers.answerHtml: The claim is false. A TCP host sweep still learns from SYN-ACK or RST even when ICMP echo is disabled; a TCP port scan can still identify listening ports. UDP sweeps may also reveal live services via application replies. Suppressing all ICMP removes some signals but also damages useful error/diagnostic behaviour. Prefer restricted exposure, segmentation, pattern detection and selective rate limiting.

tutorialAnswers.question: Q13. Explain why UDP floods do not need to establish anything before they can start doing damage, and why this makes UDP flooding cheaper for an attacker than an equivalent TCP-based flood would be.   [LO1]
tutorialAnswers.answerHtml: UDP needs no handshake or established state before a receiver processes incoming packets. Attackers can emit packets immediately, possibly with spoofed sources, consuming victim bandwidth/CPU; closed ports may also cause costly ICMP responses. This avoids connection-setup overhead. TCP SYN floods can themselves be cheap, so the useful comparison is UDP's absence of required setup, not a claim that every UDP flood is cheaper than every TCP attack.

tutorialAnswers.question: Q14. Both TCP's weaknesses and UDP's weaknesses trace back to the same underlying design assumption. State that assumption in your own words, and explain how it shows up differently in a TCP attack versus a UDP attack of your choosing.   [LO1, LO2]
tutorialAnswers.answerHtml: The underlying assumption is that the network and apparent senders are trustworthy enough to process packets without cryptographic proof at transport level. TCP tracks state but does not authenticate packet origin: a forged acceptable-sequence RST can disrupt a connection. UDP has no protocol handshake/state, so a spoofed datagram flood can make the victim spend resources immediately. Checksums do not solve either sender-authentication problem.

tutorialAnswers.question: Q15. A small business has almost no security budget this year. Using this week's mitigations, recommend three that could realistically be implemented at little to no cost, and justify why each one still meaningfully reduces risk despite costing so little.   [LO2, LO3]
tutorialAnswers.answerHtml: First, disable unused services and close their ports using existing host/router firewalls: fewer targets remain available. Second, enable supported SYN cookies: reduce classic backlog exhaustion using configuration rather than new appliances. Third, configure appropriate ingress/egress anti-spoofing and sensible existing-device rate limits: reduce forged-source abuse and unwanted load. Patch systems too. These cost administrator time, and a truly link-saturating flood can still require provider assistance.

sections.title: Firewall, IDS and IPS: what action follows a match?
sections.html:
ControlDecision basisActionRole
FirewallConfigured access policy: addresses, ports, protocols; advanced models add application/user/content contextPermit or deny trafficPreventive access enforcement
IDSSignatures, anomalies or suspicious activityGenerate alerts; a passive sensor does not itself drop trafficDetective visibility
IPSDetection logic similar to IDS, deployed in traffic pathDrop/block or otherwise prevent detected trafficActive prevention

A firewall is hardware or software enforcing traffic policy between trust boundaries. Its protection depends on rules and placement. These controls overlap in modern products and work together in a layered design. A passive IDS typically receives mirrored traffic, whereas an IPS is inline. The lecture phrase that “both can be inline” should be read as a broad product/deployment comparison, not a claim that a passive IDS inherently blocks.

sections.title: Deployment form and inspection state
sections.html:
ChoiceStrengthsLimits and fit
Hardware firewallCentral policy for a network segment; dedicated resources and often accelerated throughputUpfront appliance cost; perimeter-only placement does not see all internal east-west traffic
Software/host firewallGranular protection per host; low software cost; follows endpointUses host resources; host compromise may disable/bypass it
Stateless inspectionEach packet independently checked against header rules; fast and inexpensiveNo memory of legitimate initiation; reply-looking spoofed packets may match broad return rules
Stateful inspectionState table tracks addresses, ports, protocol and connection stage; allows valid return traffic of permitted sessionsConsumes memory/CPU; floods can exhaust state; encrypted payload remains opaque without decryption

Use hardware boundaries and endpoint software together: one protects shared paths, the other controls each host including internal traffic. State tracking is context, not proof of sender identity or a guarantee against valid-sequence on-path injection.

sections.title: Types 1–3: header, connection and session
sections.html:
TypeMechanismAdvantagesLimitationsUse case
Packet filteringL3/L4 header ACL; top-to-bottom first match; statelessFastest classic type, low cost and overhead; suitable on routersNo payload or state inspection; complex rule sets; fragment handling can create gapsBasic perimeter filtering, router ACLs, high-throughput simple policies
Stateful inspectionL3/L4 plus connection-state table; permitted new connection enables matching repliesStronger context, simpler reply rules, rejects out-of-state trafficState exhaustion and troubleshooting complexity; no inherent TLS payload visibilityOrdinary enterprise perimeter and context-aware filtering
Circuit-level gatewayLecture L5 model; verifies session establishment/legitimacy then relays traffic; SOCKS is classic exampleLighter than protocol-specific content inspection; hides internal addressingApproved session can carry malicious content; limited standalone modern useSOCKS-based proxying and conceptual building block

Return-traffic example: a stateless ACL allowing packets from source port 443 cannot tell whether an internal client previously initiated the conversation. A stateful firewall checks its connection table before accepting a reply. The state table is itself a resource requiring protection.

sections.title: Types 4–7: protocol, application, web specialism and bundles
sections.html:
TypeMechanismStrength / scenarioCost or limitation
Application-layer/proxyL7 intermediary terminates client connection, inspects protocol requests and opens a separate server connectionFine HTTP-method/FTP-command/content policies, response sanitisation and masking internal client IPs; corporate web/email proxiesHigh classic-type overhead; per-protocol support; possible bottleneck/failure point
NGFWStateful inspection + DPI + application recognition + integrated IPS; often user/group policyEnterprise application-aware control even when many applications share 443; may inspect TLS when properly configuredExpense, management complexity, decryption throughput cost and concentrated responsibility
WAFL7 HTTP/HTTPS inspection in front of a web application; signatures and/or positive allowed-request modelSpecialised defence against SQL injection, XSS and related web patterns; e-commerce portals, cloud reverse proxiesWeb-only scope; tuning creates false positives/negatives; cannot replace application controls
UTMFirewall, antivirus, IPS/IDS, content/URL filtering, VPN and sometimes anti-spam bundled in one applianceSMBs/branches get one vendor/interface and simpler deployment at lower integration costShared bottleneck and failure point; scaling and individual feature depth may be limited

NGFW versus UTM in this lecture: integrated, often single-pass engine versus separately bundled security modules. Actual products can overlap, so evaluate measured throughput with required features enabled, management effort and failure handling. A WAF must see HTTP plaintext through TLS termination/decryption or an equivalent integration; an encrypted stream cannot simply be inspected by naming it HTTPS.

sections.title: Why each generation emerged
sections.html:
• Late 1980s packet filters met basic access-control needs with limited processing power.
  • 1994 Check Point FireWall-1 is the lecture milestone for stateful inspection: track conversations to close context gaps.
  • 1990s circuit gateways and application proxies explored session validation versus deeper protocol interpretation.
  • 2000s UTM reduced the burden of integrating many separate products.
  • Roughly 2007–2010 onward, NGFW application awareness/integrated prevention addressed applications sharing common ports, particularly HTTPS. WAF developed as specialised web protection.

The analytical arc is header → connection → protocol → application/user and sometimes decrypted content. More context can improve precision and visibility, but consumes processing, configuration effort and budget. WAF goes narrower/deeper; UTM goes wider across functions. These are capability trade-offs rather than a strict ranking in which every later device replaces all earlier ones.

sections.title: Recommendation method for structured answers
sections.html:
State the requirement and choose the control that inspects the relevant information. A router ACL cannot distinguish SQL code inside an allowed HTTP request. A WAF can inspect that application pattern, while the network firewall still controls reachability. For content sanitisation and hidden client addressing, choose an application proxy; for a small branch needing multiple manageable functions, consider UTM; for enterprise application/user policy, consider NGFW.

Then state one benefit, one cost and a complementary measure. Performance must be considered with real features enabled. Keep systems/apps patched, apply least privilege and monitor alerts; buying a firewall does not make an unsafe application safe.

quiz.question: A sensor sees malicious traffic and sends an alert but cannot block it. It is acting as:
quiz.explanation: An IDS is detective; an IPS adds inline prevention.

quiz.question: Which firewall automatically associates allowed outbound sessions with return traffic?
quiz.explanation: The state table supplies connection context for permitted replies.

quiz.question: Which classic type terminates the client connection and creates a separate connection to the destination?
quiz.explanation: The proxy understands the application protocol and acts as an intermediary.

quiz.question: A firewall allows TCP 443, and SQL injection passes inside HTTPS after decryption at the server. Best additional specialist control?
options: WAF at the web application boundary
quiz.explanation: A WAF inspects web request/response patterns; L3/L4 permission alone does not assess SQL injection.

quiz.question: Which statement best reflects the lecture NGFW/UTM contrast?
options: NGFW emphasises integrated inspection; UTM emphasises bundled functions
quiz.explanation: This is a conceptual architectural distinction; actual vendor capabilities overlap.

quiz.question: What can pass through a circuit-level gateway after a valid session is approved?
options: Malicious content it does not inspect
quiz.explanation: It verifies sessions, not payload safety.

quiz.question: For a small branch with limited budget and no dedicated security staff, what is a strong lecture-based choice?
options: UTM, after checking performance and failure risks
Maximum separate vendors regardless of staffing
No firewall because traffic is encrypted
quiz.explanation: UTM offers broad functions and one management interface, with bottleneck/depth trade-offs.

quiz.question: What is a resource-exhaustion risk introduced by stateful inspection?
options: A reduction to zero header fields
quiz.explanation: Tracking flows consumes finite state; connection floods can exhaust it.

tutorialAnswers.question: Q1. Explain the difference between a firewall, an IDS, and an IPS, specifically in terms of what each one actually does once it identifies something suspicious.   [LO4]
tutorialAnswers.answerHtml: A firewall permits or denies according to configured access policy. An IDS recognises suspicious signatures/anomalies and alerts without directly blocking in its passive role. An IPS is inline and can drop/block the detected attack. Modern NGFW/UTM products may combine these functions, but the action distinction remains important.

tutorialAnswers.question: Q2. Explain the difference between a software firewall and a hardware firewall, and why most real networks deploy both together rather than choosing one over the other.   [LO4]
tutorialAnswers.answerHtml: A hardware firewall is a network appliance providing central, often accelerated enforcement without using endpoint CPU; it costs more and sees traffic that traverses it. A software firewall protects a host with granular local rules and often little software cost, but uses host resources and may be undermined by host compromise. Combining them protects perimeter paths and endpoint/internal traffic.

tutorialAnswers.question: Q3. Explain the difference between stateless and stateful inspection, and describe one specific scenario where a stateless firewall's lack of context becomes a genuine vulnerability.   [LO4]
tutorialAnswers.answerHtml: Stateless inspection compares isolated packet headers to static rules. Stateful inspection maintains connection context and permits valid returns to allowed sessions. A stateless rule permitting inbound packets merely because their source port is 443 could accept a spoofed unsolicited packet from that port; the firewall has no prior-connection record to distinguish it from a real web reply.

tutorialAnswers.question: Q4. Distinguish Packet Filtering from Stateful Inspection specifically in terms of how each treats return traffic for a connection that was originally initiated from inside the network.   [LO4]
tutorialAnswers.answerHtml: A packet filter needs static rules for both directions and cannot prove an inbound reply belongs to a session initiated internally. A stateful firewall checks the initiating packet against policy, records the flow and automatically allows valid return packets matching that state, reducing the need for broad return-direction rules.

tutorialAnswers.question: Q5. Explain what a Circuit-Level Gateway actually validates, and why it provides no protection against malicious content once a session has already been approved.   [LO3]
tutorialAnswers.answerHtml: It validates a legitimate session setup, such as the TCP handshake in the lecture's circuit-gateway model, then relays without understanding later payload content. Therefore an attacker communicating over an approved session can send malicious content unless another control inspects the application. Address hiding does not imply payload safety.

tutorialAnswers.question: Q6. A company wants deep content filtering, such as blocking specific content inside an HTTP request, and strong anonymisation of its internal users' identities. Evaluate whether an Application-Layer/Proxy firewall or a simple Stateful Inspection firewall is the better fit, and justify your answer.   [LO4]
tutorialAnswers.answerHtml: Choose an application-layer/proxy firewall. It terminates the internal connection, interprets HTTP requests, applies fine content policies and opens a separate external connection, masking the internal client IP. A basic stateful firewall knows connection context but not request-body semantics. The proxy needs protocol support and incurs higher processing/latency costs; its masking is not a guarantee of total user anonymity.

tutorialAnswers.question: Q7. Distinguish NGFW from UTM. Both bundle multiple security functions together, so what is the key architectural difference between them, and what trade-off does that difference actually create?   [LO4]
tutorialAnswers.answerHtml: The lecture describes NGFW as a tightly integrated application-aware inspection/IPS architecture, often processing traffic in a coordinated engine; UTM packages several distinct security modules under one appliance/interface. NGFW can provide deeper contextual integration but at higher cost and management complexity. UTM simplifies broad deployment, often for SMBs, with potential shared bottlenecks and less specialist depth. Real product boundaries overlap.
